title: Research methods
examples: When should I use numbers versus words in my research?
What is the difference between making sure my study is valid and reliable?
Can you give me an example of a qualitative study?

explain.say: Today we will look at different research methods you can use.
Quantitative research uses numbers to test specific ideas.
Qualitative research explores deep meanings through words and observations.
Validity means your study measures what it is supposed to measure.
Reliability means if you repeat the study, you get similar results.
For example, measuring student anxiety levels is a good real-life test.

faq.q: When should I use numbers versus words in my research?
faq.a: Use numbers when you need to count or measure things across many people. Use words when you need to understand why people feel a certain way.
asks: Do I need stats or stories?
Should I use surveys or interviews?

faq.q: What is the difference between making sure my study is valid and reliable?
faq.a: Validity checks if your tool measures the right thing. Reliability checks if your tool gives the same answer every time you use it.
asks: If it's reliable, is it valid?

faq.q: If my study is reliable but not valid, what does that mean?
faq.a: It means your measurements are consistent, but they are consistently measuring the wrong thing. For example, measuring height with a ruler meant for weight.
asks: What if I get the same wrong answer?

faq.q: Do I need to be perfect in both validity and reliability?
faq.a: While both are important, achieving high reliability is often a necessary first step toward achieving validity.
asks: Which one is more important for a first paper?

faq.q: Can a study be both quantitative and qualitative?
faq.a: Yes, this is called mixed methods research. You might use numbers to show how many people feel something, and words to show what they mean.

facts: Quantitative research often uses statistical analysis on numerical data.
Qualitative research often involves interviews and textual analysis.
Validity concerns whether the research tool measures the intended concept.
Reliability concerns the consistency of the measurement results over time.

quiz.say: A researcher counts the number of times students use their phones during class.
quiz.why: Counting is a numerical measurement, which belongs to quantitative research.

wrong.0: This confuses the measurement type with the consistency check.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you are studying student behavior, which can seem descriptive.
wrong.3: This option confuses the type of data with the quality check itself.

quiz.say: A researcher asks students to write detailed essays about their experience with online learning.
quiz.why: Essays provide rich, descriptive text that requires interpretation of meaning.

wrong.0: This confuses the data type with the consistency check.
wrong.2: This is tempting because it involves a large group of students.
wrong.3: This confuses the data type with the quality check.

quiz.say: If a test gives different scores every time it is given to the same person, the test lacks:
quiz.why: Reliability specifically addresses whether results are consistent upon repeated testing.

wrong.1: Validity is about measuring the right thing, not about consistency.
wrong.2: This suggests a data type, not a property of the test.
wrong.3: This suggests a research design, not a measure of consistency.
